title: Horses of Fire at Dothan; Famine in Samaria
summary: Elisha makes a lost iron axe head float for one of the sons of the prophets. When the king of Aram learns that Elisha is warning Israel's king of his plans, he sends an army to seize the prophet at Dothan, but the LORD opens the eyes of Elisha's servant to see the hills full of horses and chariots of fire, strikes the Arameans with blindness, and Elisha leads them into Samaria, where they are fed and sent home. Later Ben-hadad besieges Samaria, famine drives mothers to eat their children, and the king vows to kill Elisha.
story: The chapter moves from the smallest miracle in the Elisha cycle to the largest crisis. It continues the war with Aram that lay in the background of chapter 5, but now Elisha is not healing an Aramean general; he is the target of an Aramean army. The theme that links its scenes is sight. The servant cannot see the heavenly army until his eyes are opened; the Aramean soldiers are blinded and then made to see where they are; and the king of Israel, faced with the horror of the siege, sees only that the LORD is to blame. The chapter ends mid-crisis, and chapter 7 brings the resolution Elisha promises.
historical:
The kings are again unnamed except for Ben-hadad of Aram in verse 24. Ben-hadad, meaning son of Hadad (the storm god), seems to have been a name or throne name used by more than one king of Damascus, and the one here is often identified as the king who fought Ahab in 1 Kings 20. Assyrian records from the 850s and 840s name the king of Damascus as Hadadezer, and scholars debate whether he is the biblical Ben-hadad under another name or whether the biblical accounts have been arranged differently; the question remains open. The king of Israel is most likely Jehoram son of Ahab, whose reign ended in 841 BC.

Dothan, on the main route from the Jezreel Valley south into the hill country, lay about ten miles north of Samaria; it is the place where Joseph's brothers sold him (Genesis 37:17). Samaria, the capital Omri had built on a steep, isolated hill, was strongly fortified and could not be easily stormed, so an enemy's best weapon was starvation. Sieges could last months or years; Samaria would later hold out for three years against Assyria (17:5).
cultural:
Iron tools were valuable in Israel in this period, and a borrowed axe head could not easily be replaced by a poor member of a prophetic community; losing it meant a debt he could not pay. In warfare, captives could be killed or enslaved by the captor, and the king of Israel's eager question, “My father, shall I kill them?” (verse 21), assumes that option. Elisha's answer appeals to a custom of mercy: even captives taken in battle were not necessarily killed, still less men delivered by God's action rather than by the king's own sword. A shared meal in the ancient Near East created obligations of peace between host and guest.

The siege prices in verse 25 are grim. A donkey was an unclean animal under Israel's law, and its head held little meat, yet it sold for eighty shekels of silver. Dove's dung may be meant literally, as fuel or desperate food, or it may be a popular name for some poor food such as a kind of seed pod; interpreters are not sure. The cannibalism of verses 28-29 fulfills the covenant curses of Leviticus 26:29 and Deuteronomy 28:53-57, which warned that a people who abandoned the LORD would come to this in siege. The king's sackcloth under his robes (verse 30) was a sign of mourning and penitence, worn out of sight.
literary: The chapter contains three episodes joined by the figure of Elisha and by the theme of seeing. The axe head story (verses 1-7) shows the prophet's care for a single anxious man. The Dothan story (verses 8-23) is built on a play of eyes: Elisha prays “please open his eyes that he may see” (verse 17), then asks the LORD to strike the Arameans with blindness, then to open their eyes again in Samaria. The irony is sharp: the army sent to capture the prophet is captured by him, and the people who come to seize him are led by him. The siege story (verses 24-33) opens with the note that Aramean raiders no longer came, and then shows something far worse: a full-scale siege. Its central scene, the woman's appeal to the king, echoes Solomon's judgment between two mothers (1 Kings 3), but where Solomon's wisdom brought justice, this king can do nothing. The final verse is unclear in Hebrew about who speaks, the messenger or the king, but the words express the despair of the court.

outline.t: Elisha reveals the king of Aram's plans
Surrounded at Dothan; the servant's eyes opened
The Arameans blinded, led to Samaria, fed, and released
The siege of Samaria and the king's vow
The king's messenger comes to Elisha's house

doctrines.note: God's care stretches from a borrowed axe head to the protection of a city. His help is often invisible, as the servant learns: “those who are with us are more than those who are with them” (verse 16).
Elisha's prayers are short and specific: open his eyes, strike them with blindness, open their eyes. Prayer here does not change what God is doing so much as it asks God to let people see it.
The famine in Samaria is the covenant curse coming true. The king blames Elisha and the LORD, but the siege is the fruit of the nation's long unfaithfulness, as Leviticus and Deuteronomy had warned.

words.note: Paqach, to open, used almost only of opening eyes. It appears four times here: the servant's eyes are opened to see the heavenly army, and the blinded soldiers' eyes are opened to see they are in Samaria. The same verb is used when Hagar's eyes were opened to see a well (Genesis 21:19). It is God's act of granting sight.

Sanwerim, blindness, a rare word used elsewhere only of the men of Sodom struck at Lot's door (Genesis 19:11). Some think it means dazzling or confusion rather than total loss of sight, since the soldiers follow Elisha without recognizing him or the road. Either way, God disables the attackers without killing them.

Yasha, to save, help, or deliver. The woman cries to the king, help me, and he answers that if the LORD does not help her he has nothing to give (verses 26-27). The king is right about the source of help but wrong in his despair. The same root gives the names Joshua, Elisha, and Jesus.

christ: Elisha's refusal to kill the captured Arameans and his command to feed them anticipate Jesus' teaching to love enemies and do good to those who hate you (Luke 6:27-35), and Paul's instruction, drawn from Proverbs 25:21-22, to feed a hungry enemy (Romans 12:20). The heavenly army around Elisha has a counterpart in Gethsemane, where Jesus tells Peter he could call on his Father for more than twelve legions of angels but will not, because he has come to drink the cup (Matthew 26:53-54). The opening of blind eyes is one of the signs of the Messiah in Isaiah 35:5 and 61:1 (as the Greek version reads), and Jesus both gives sight to the blind and, after his resurrection, opens the eyes of the two disciples at Emmaus to recognize him (Luke 24:31). These are thematic echoes rather than predictions, but they show the same God at work who opens eyes and spares enemies.

hard.q: Why does the Bible record something as horrific as mothers eating their children, and why does the king blame God?
hard.a: The scene is meant to be horrifying, and the narrator does not soften it. It is included because it is the fulfillment of what the covenant warned: Leviticus 26:29 and Deuteronomy 28:53-57 described exactly this as the end of a people who abandoned the LORD, and Lamentations 4:10 records it again in Jerusalem's fall. The Bible does not present it as God's desire but as the depth of misery that follows when a nation rejects its only protection and is left to its enemies. The king's response is revealing. He has put on sackcloth, a sign of mourning or repentance, yet he blames the prophet and then the LORD. Some interpreters think he blamed Elisha because the prophet had counseled waiting on the LORD and resisting surrender; others think he simply lashed out at God's representative. Either way, the chapter shows a man who grieves the consequences of sin without turning from it. The next chapter shows that the LORD had not abandoned the city even then.

questions: Elisha's servant saw only the enemy army until his eyes were opened. What situations in your life might look different if you could see what God sees?
Elisha told the king to feed his captured enemies rather than kill them. What would it look like to treat someone who has opposed you with that kind of mercy?
The king wore sackcloth yet said, “Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?” How can outward signs of repentance coexist with a heart that has given up on God?
